title: API styles: REST, GraphQL, gRPC
summary: Pick the style that fits your clients: public web and mobile apps, flexible data needs, or fast internal service calls.

values.rest: Resources addressed by URL and manipulated with HTTP methods
values.graphql: Clients query a typed schema and ask for exactly the fields they need
values.grpc: Remote procedure calls defined in a schema (Protocol Buffers)

values.rest: Easy with HTTP caching and CDNs
values.graphql: Harder: usually one POST endpoint, needs custom caching

values.grpc: Built-in client, server and bidirectional streams
Needs a proxy such as gRPC-Web

rest: Public APIs, simple CRUD and anything benefiting from HTTP caching.
You want the broadest tooling and easiest adoption.
graphql: Many client types need different slices of related data.
You want to reduce round trips for complex screens.
grpc: Internal service-to-service calls needing low latency and strict contracts.
You need streaming or polyglot services with generated clients.

watchOut: GraphQL can hide expensive queries: add depth, cost and rate limits.
Do not expose gRPC directly to browsers without a gateway.

title: Real-time updates: long polling, SSE, WebSocket
summary: Choose how the server delivers new data to clients without them asking every second.

values.long-poll: Server to client, one response per request
A new HTTP request after each response
Works through almost any proxy and load balancer
values.ws: Needs proxy and load balancer support and sticky routing

values.sse: Built in with last event id

long-poll: You need compatibility with restrictive networks.
Updates are infrequent and a simple fallback is enough.
sse: Updates flow one way, such as feeds, notifications or progress.
You want simple, resilient streaming over HTTP.
ws: You need low-latency two-way messaging such as chat or collaboration.

watchOut: Persistent connections make deployments and scaling stateful: plan connection draining and a message backplane.
Always handle reconnection and missed messages.

title: Monolith vs microservices
summary: Decide how to split your system into deployable units, trading team autonomy against operational complexity.

values.monolith: Fast: one codebase, simple local setup
values.micro: Slower: service boundaries, contracts and infrastructure first

values.monolith: A bug or overload can take down everything
values.micro: Faults can be contained, but cascades across calls are possible

values.monolith: One database and transactions are easy
values.micro: Data owned per service; cross-service work needs sagas or eventual consistency
High: discovery, tracing, versioning, many pipelines

monolith: A small team and an evolving product where boundaries are not yet clear.
You want speed and simplicity until a real pain appears.
micro: Many teams need to ship independently.
Parts of the system have very different scaling or reliability needs.

watchOut: A distributed monolith: services so coupled they must deploy together.
A well-structured modular monolith is often the best starting point.

title: Synchronous calls vs asynchronous messaging
summary: Decide whether a request waits for downstream work or hands it off through a queue.

values.sync: Waits for the result, simple to reason about
values.async: Gets an acknowledgement; the result arrives later

values.sync: Caller depends on the callee being up and fast
values.async: Loosely coupled in time; producer and consumer fail independently

values.sync: Spikes hit the downstream service directly
values.async: A queue absorbs bursts and smooths the load
Retries, dead-letter queues and idempotent consumers
Eventually consistent; ordering and duplicates need care

sync: The user needs the result immediately to continue.
The work is quick and the dependency is reliable.
async: The work is slow, bursty or can happen after responding.
You want producers isolated from consumer outages.

watchOut: Retrying synchronous calls without backoff and jitter can amplify an outage.
Async still needs idempotency: messages can be delivered more than once.
